series.title: The Wrong Hire
series.tagline: ADHD, misfits, and security engineering in the agentic world.

featuredPost.title: The Wrong Hire
paragraphs: I was listening to a recent podcast on my walk and it made me think about how my early days of being "difficult to manage" turned into a competitive advantage in our ever-changing AI environment.

I heard how one company 2x'd engineering throughput in nine months. Their lead engineer calls the last three months "the most fun of my career." Their CI system melted from the volume. They fixed it and kept going.

The people driving results are no longer the ones who thrive on predictability and long planning cycles. We're the ones who can't stop asking "and then what?" Who hyperfocus until the problem breaks, then jump to the next thing. Who find chaos energizing rather than paralyzing.
That's not a disorder. That's the job description in our current agentic world. Our imagination is the bottleneck now, not the tools, not the headcount, not the sprint capacity.

Moving fast doesn't mean ignoring security. It means breaking everything deliberately to push the boundaries of "what does this button do?" (in a controlled environment, on purpose) and carrying the lessons back to production and the security teams. The chaos people aren't reckless. They've already broken it twice in the lab before you've finished your threat model.

The environment that punished us for being everywhere at once is over. Backlog zero, frictionless flows, and secure data are the real goals, and those of us who'll hit them first were never comfortable sitting still anyway.

series.title: What Free Services Collect About You
series.tagline: The trade you didn't know you made: Google, Meta, Apple, Spotify, Amazon.

featuredPost.title: Intro: the trade you didn't know you made
paragraphs: You aren't the customer. You're the product. You've heard that. But do you actually know what product you are?
Every "free" app you use runs servers, employs engineers, and pays for bandwidth. That isn't charity. It's a trade, and you're on the wrong end of it.
This is a seven-part series about what Google, Meta, Apple, Spotify, and Amazon actually collect about you. Not in theory. In practice. What they store, what they infer, and what they do with it.

posts.title: Intro: the trade you didn't know you made
posts.hook: You aren't the customer. You're the product. But do you know what product you are?
posts.body:
You aren't the customer. You're the product. You've heard that. But do you actually know what product you are?

Every "free" app you use runs servers, employs engineers, and pays for bandwidth. That isn't charity. It's a trade, and you're on the wrong end of it.

This is a seven-part series about what Google, Meta, Apple, Spotify, and Amazon actually collect about you. Not in theory. In practice. What they store, what they infer, and what they do with it.

The numbers will bother you. Not because they're secret. Most of it is buried in terms of service you clicked through in 2014. It bothers you because when you see it laid out, you realize you handed it over voluntarily, in exchange for a maps app and a photo filter.

We'll take them one at a time. By the end, you'll either delete everything, or you'll make a deliberate choice to keep using them. Either way, at least it'll be a choice.

posts.title: Google: there's a lot of you in there
posts.hook: Search, location, voice, purchases. A decade of you, cross-referenced.

posts.title: Meta: they mapped your psychology
posts.hook: Not just what you clicked. What you hovered over and didn't.

posts.title: Apple: a low bar
posts.hook: Better than the others isn't the same as good.

posts.title: Spotify: they mapped your inner life
posts.hook: Your mood, your routine, your 2am playlist. All signal.

posts.title: Amazon: a genuinely impressive business model
posts.hook: They monetize the intent to buy before you've decided to.

posts.title: Summary: make sure it's a decision
posts.hook: Delete everything, or keep it on purpose. Either way, choose.
